Title: QB-LIF: Learnable-Scale Quantized Burst Neurons for Efficient SNNs
Text:
QB-LIF: Learnable-Scale Quantized Burst Neurons for Efficient SNNs
Dewei Bai
Hongxiang Peng
Jiajun Mei
Yang Ren
Hong Qu
Dawen Xia
Zhang Yi
Abstract
Binary spike coding enables sparse and event-driven com-
putation in spiking neural networks (SNNs), yet its 1-
bit-per-timestep representation fundamentally limits in-
formation throughput. This bottleneck becomes increas-
ingly restrictive in deep architectures under short sim-
ulation horizons. We propose the Quantized Burst-LIF
(QB-LIF) neuron, which reformulates burst spiking as a
saturated uniform quantization of membrane potentials
with a learnable scale. Instead of relying on predefined
multi-threshold structures, QB-LIF treats the quantiza-
tion scale as a trainable parameter, allowing each layer to
autonomously adapt its spiking resolution to the underly-
ing membrane-potential statistics. To preserve hardware
efficiency, we introduce an absorbable scale strategy that
folds the learned quantized scale into synaptic weights dur-
ing inference, maintaining a strict accumulate-only (AC)
execution paradigm. To enable stable optimization in the
discrete multi-level space, we further design ReLSG-ET,
a rectified-linear surrogate gradient with exponential tails
that sustains gradient flow across burst intervals. Exten-
sive experiments on static (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet) and
event-driven (CIFAR10-DVS, DVS128-Gesture) bench-
marks demonstrate that QB-LIF consistently outperforms
binary and fixed-burst SNNs, achieving higher accuracy
under ultra-low latency while preserving neuromorphic
compatibility.
Keywords: Spiking Neural Network; burst spiking; learn-
able quantization; low-latency inference; surrogate func-
tion

Introduction
Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are widely regarded as
a promising paradigm for energy-efficient neuromorphic
computing, owing to their event-driven processing mech-
anism. Unlike Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) that
rely on continuous-valued activations and energy-intensive
multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, SNNs communi-
cate via sparse spike events and can be efficiently executed
on neuromorphic hardware such as Loihi [1] and Tian-
jic [2]. On such platforms, synaptic computation reduces
to low-power accumulate (AC) operations, offering the
potential for orders-of-magnitude improvements in energy
efficiency [3].
Despite this advantage, the strict binary nature of con-
ventional spiking neurons introduces a fundamental infor-
mation bottleneck. A binary spike conveys at most one
bit of information per timestep, which is drastically lower
than the representational capacity of real-valued activa-
tions in ANNs [4]. As a result, directly trained SNNs
often suffer from severe quantization loss and struggle to
achieve competitive performance on complex visual recog-
nition tasks, such as ImageNet, unless long simulation
horizons are employed. However, increasing the number
of timesteps inevitably undermines the latency and energy
advantages that motivate SNNs in the first place.
To alleviate this bottleneck, recent studies have ex-
plored burst spiking or multi-level spiking neurons, which
allow a neuron to emit multiple spikes within a single
timestep.
These approaches effectively extend the bi-
nary spike representation to discrete multi-level outputs
and have demonstrated encouraging performance improve-
ments. However, most existing methods remain rooted
in a threshold-centric design philosophy. Representative
works, such as multi-level spiking neurons [5] and integer-
valued LIF neurons [6], typically rely on fixed, equidistant
threshold sets or predefined integer spiking levels shared
across layers.
From a representational perspective, such designs im-
plicitly impose a uniform quantization rule on membrane
potentials, yet without explicitly modeling or optimiz-
ing the associated quantization scale. Crucially, treating
burst levels as fixed hyperparameters overlooks the in-
herent layer-wise heterogeneity of feature distributions in
deep SNNs, where early layers often require fine-grained
sensitivity to input variations, while deeper layers operate
over substantially different dynamic ranges. Consequently,
a globally fixed spiking granularity can lead to either pre-
mature saturation or excessive information loss, limiting
the effectiveness of burst-based spiking models.
In this work, we revisit burst spiking from a quanti-
zation perspective and propose Quantized Burst Leaky
Integrate-and-Fire (QB-LIF) neurons. Instead of treating
burst spiking as a byproduct of multiple hand-crafted
thresholds, we explicitly model burst spiking as a satu-
rated uniform quantization of membrane potentials with
a learnable scale. Specifically, a single scale parameter γ
controls both the quantization granularity of burst levels
and the effective contribution of each emitted spike. By
integrating γ into the computational graph, the spiking
resolution of each layer can be optimized end-to-end via
backpropagation, allowing the network to automatically

adapt its representational precision to task demands.
Crucially, we further introduce an absorbable scale strat-
egy, through which the learned quantization scale is folded
into synaptic weights during inference. This design decou-
ples training-time flexibility from inference-time efficiency:
while QB-LIF benefits from multi-level burst represen-
tations during learning, the deployed network preserves
a strictly accumulate-only execution paradigm without
introducing additional MAC operations or control flow.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
• We reinterpret burst spiking as an explicit uniform
quantization of membrane potentials and propose the
Quantized Burst-LIF (QB-LIF) neuron, establishing a
learnable quantization framework for adaptive multi-
level spike representations.
• We introduce a layer-wise learnable quantization scale
together with an absorbable scale strategy, enabling
adaptive spiking resolution during training while pre-
serving strict accumulate-only (AC) inference for neu-
romorphic deployment.
• We design ReLSG-ET, a surrogate gradient with expo-
nential tails, to ensure stable optimization in discrete
multi-level burst spaces.
• Extensive evaluations on static and event-driven
benchmarks validate that adaptive quantized burst
representations substantially enhance representa-
tional capacity under ultra-low latency while main-
taining event-driven sparsity and hardware compati-
bility.
2
Related Work
2.1
SNN Training Paradigms
Training methods for Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs)
primarily fall into two categories: ANN-to-SNN conversion
and direct training. ANN-to-SNN Conversion leverages
parameters from pre-trained ANNs to circumvent training
difficulties. Techniques such as weight scaling, threshold
balancing [7], and soft-reset mechanisms [7] have success-
fully mapped analog ReLU activations to spike rates in
deep architectures. Advanced optimization strategies, in-
cluding quantization clip-floor-shift (QCFS) [8] and layer-
wise calibration [9], align spiking rates with ANN activa-
tions to achieve high accuracy. However, this paradigm
largely treats spikes as rate-based approximations of static
values, and often does not explicitly exploit fine-grained
temporal dynamics, requiring long simulation windows to
reduce quantization error. Direct Training utilizes sur-
rogate gradients to address the non-differentiability of
spike generation [10]. By introducing differentiable ap-
proximations for membrane potentials [11] and enforcing
joint optimization of spatial and temporal dynamics (e.g.,
STBP [12]), these methods significantly reduce latency.
Our work adopts the direct training paradigm to fully
leverage the temporal efficiency of SNNs. In addition to
training paradigms, several works enhance SNN perfor-
mance through architectural adaptations. Wang et al. [13]
proposed SpikeGoogle, which integrates a GoogLeNet-
style inception module into a spiking framework to capture
multi-scale spatial features within spiking convolutional
layers. Such approaches focus on structural enrichment
of spatial representations rather than modifying the spike
coding mechanism itself.
2.2
Burst Spiking Dynamics
Binary spike coding fundamentally limits the information
throughput of spiking neurons, which has motivated a
series of studies aiming to mitigate quantization-induced
information loss. Early efforts mainly focus on rectify-
ing the membrane potential distribution prior to bina-
rization, including InfLoR-SNN [14], IM-Loss [15], and
RecDis-SNN [16]. These methods alleviate information
degradation at the distribution level, yet the spike out-
put remains binary and thus intrinsically bounded by a
1-bit-per-timestep representational capacity.
Beyond distribution rectification, several works extend
the discrete spiking space of spiking neurons. Ternary
Spikes [4] introduce signed spike states {−1, 0, 1}, provid-
ing a modest increase in expressiveness while still relying
on a fixed and low-cardinality output space. However,
such limited extensions remain insufficient for modeling
the wide dynamic ranges encountered in deep spiking
networks.
More expressive spiking behaviors have been explored
through multi-level or burst-based spiking mechanisms.
Multi-Level spiking (MLF) [5] enables neurons to emit
multiple spikes within a single timestep by employing fixed,
equidistant thresholds. While MLF increases representa-
tional capacity, its rigid threshold design lacks adaptability
to layer-wise heterogeneity in deep architectures. Related
integer-valued training paradigms, such as I-LIF [6], op-
timize networks using integer activations and decompose
them into spike trains at inference. Similarly, Spike-driven
Transformer [17] adopts spiking approximations to facil-
itate large-scale SNN training, but primarily focuses on
architectural scaling rather than learning adaptive spike
quantization levels.
Fan et al. [18] propose a multi-synaptic spiking neuron
that enhances representational capacity by introducing
parallel synaptic pathways with independent thresholds
and dynamics. By distributing spiking responses across
multiple synaptic channels, this model improves spatiotem-
poral information encoding without relying on high spiking
rates. At a phenomenological level, such synaptic paral-
lelism also increases the information carried by individual
spike events, yielding effects partially analogous to burst
spiking, but realized through structural expansion at the
synaptic level rather than neuron-level multi-spike emis-
sion.
2


In parallel, burst spiking has been explored in ANN-
to-SNN conversion frameworks [19, 20, 21], where burst
spikes are leveraged to reduce conversion error and resid-
ual information loss. By permitting a neuron to emit
multiple spikes within a single timestep, these methods
effectively compress the simulation time required for ac-
curate inference. However, these approaches inherit the
limitations of conversion-based pipelines and do not fully
exploit burst dynamics during direct SNN training.
Existing burst spiking methods implicitly implement
a uniform quantization through fixed threshold spacing.
However, the quantization step size is treated as a pre-
defined structural constant rather than an optimizable
parameter. As a result, spiking granularity remains man-
ually specified and cannot adapt to layer-wise membrane-
potential statistics.
2.3
Surrogate Gradients for Discrete Spik-
ing
Surrogate gradient methods [10] are essential for train-
ing SNNs. Classical functions include rectangular (box-
car) [12, 22], sigmoid, and arctan variants [23]. While
effective for binary neurons, they face limitations when
the membrane potential spans multiple threshold inter-
vals, as in burst neurons. Smooth surrogates (e.g., Arctan)
decay rapidly away from the threshold, causing gradient
starvation for upper-level burst intervals where potentials
are large. Rectangular surrogates provide stable flow but
introduce abrupt cutoffs, destabilizing learning when mem-
brane potentials shift between quantization bins during
the optimization of learnable thresholds.
Taken together, prior studies have explored efficient
training paradigms, enhanced spike representations, and
surrogate gradient designs largely in isolation. Conversion-
based methods emphasize accuracy but incur long tem-
poral windows, while direct training approaches improve
latency yet remain constrained by limited spike expres-
siveness. Meanwhile, existing burst and multi-level spik-
ing schemes increase capacity through fixed structures
or architecture-specific approximations, and surrogate
gradients are predominantly tailored to binary spiking
regimes. In contrast, our work reconsiders quantization
as an intrinsic spiking mechanism within neuron dynam-
ics, conceptually distinguishing it from prior approaches
that treat integer-valued or multi-level spiking as train-
ing or inference approximations, and thereby providing a
quantization-oriented perspective for adaptive and expres-
sive spike-based representations.

Burst spiking arises as a consequence of quantized
membrane-potential discretization. The enhanced rep-
resentational granularity introduced by multi-threshold
quantization is depicted in Fig. 1((b)). To analyze this
effect formally, we consider the deterministic multi-level
quantization mapping from the membrane potential U to
the discrete spike variable Sburst. Inserting the ascending
thresholds Vth = {1, 2, . . . , Nmax} partitions the voltage
axis so that the burst spiking Sburst ∈{0, 1, . . . , Nmax}
counts thresholds crossed. It is easy to obtain that the
mutual information of burst spiking is bounded by

allocation of quantization resolution across layers.
4.3
Quantized Burst Leaky Integrate-and-
Fire Neuron
To address the information bottleneck of spiking neuron,
we propose the Quantized Burst Leaky Integrate-and-Fire
(QB-LIF) neuron, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Unlike conven-
tional burst or multi-threshold neurons that rely on prede-
fined or heuristically adjusted spiking thresholds, QB-LIF
explicitly models burst spiking as a uniform quantization
of membrane potentials with a learnable scale. This for-
mulation elevates burst spiking from a threshold-design
problem to a representation-learning problem that can be
optimized end-to-end.

4.4
Surrogate Gradients for Quantized
Burst Spiking
The activation behavior and corresponding surrogate gradi-
ent are summarized in Fig. 3. Quantized burst spiking sub-
stantially enhances the representational capacity of spiking
neurons, but it poses significant challenges for gradient-
based optimization due to the non-differentiability of the
underlying quantization operator. Specifically, the burst
output is generated via a floor-based quantization, whose
exact derivative with respect to the membrane potential
is zero almost everywhere and undefined at quantization
boundaries.

As illustrated in Fig. 3(b), this surrogate yields a

burst levels, thereby preventing gradient starvation in

a single threshold and rapidly vanish elsewhere, which
becomes inadequate for multi-level burst representations.
Unlike approaches that rescale spike amplitudes[4, 15],
the proposed formulation treats γ(ℓ) as a quantization
parameter acting directly on membrane potentials. By
optimizing γ(ℓ) in a layer-wise manner, the network can
adaptively adjust the quantization resolution during train-
ing according to the membrane-potential distribution of
each layer, jointly shaping burst representation granularity
and the effective support of surrogate gradient propagation
without relying on manually designed thresholds.
5
Experiments
We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effec-
tiveness of the proposed QB-LIF and compare it against
recent state-of-the-art SNN training methods. Evaluations
are performed on both static and event-based benchmarks
to assess generalization across different input modalities.
For static image recognition, we use CIFAR-10, CI-
FAR 100 [32], and ImageNet [33].
For neuromorphic
vision tasks, we adopt CIFAR10 DVS [34] and DVS128-
Gesture [35], which are widely used benchmarks in event-
driven perception.
We evaluate QB-LIF on multiple representative archi-
tectures, including ResNet-18 [23], ResNet-19 [36], and
ResNet-20 [37], following standard SNN design practices.
For fair comparison, we adopt the same data preprocessing
and augmentation strategies as in prior work, including
dataset-specific normalization, random horizontal flipping
and cropping, AutoAugment [38], and Cutout [39].
Optimization is performed using SGD or AdamW with
a cosine annealing learning rate schedule, depending on
the dataset and architecture. All experiments are con-
ducted on a workstation equipped with an AMD EPYC
7282 16-core CPU and 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Detailed
training configurations and hyperparameters for ImageNet
experiments are summarized in Table 1.

CIFAR
We evaluate prior methods on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-

inference latency and energy consumption.
Directly trained SNN approaches, including RecDis-

and remain constrained by the limited representational
capacity of spike coding.

state-of-the-art results while operating at even lower la-

Ablation Study
To disentangle the effects of burst representation and
surrogate gradient design, we conduct an ablation study
on CIFAR10 using ResNet-20 trained directly as an SNN
with a simulation duration of 2 timesteps. The results are
summarized in Table 5.
Effect of Multi-Level Spike Representation
We
first compare conventional Binary LIF with integer-based
spike formulations under the same Box-ET surrogate. Re-
placing binary spikes with multi-level spike representa-
tion (I-LIF (Box-ET)) improves accuracy from 90.50%
to 94.85%, demonstrating that multi-level spike signaling
significantly enhances representational capacity under a
short simulation duration.
Effect of Quantized Burst Encoding
Next, we eval-
uate the impact of the proposed quantized burst formula-
tion. Under the same surrogate, QB-LIF further improves
accuracy to (93.85% →95.05% for Box-ET and 94.45%
→95.58% for ReLSG-ET), compared with I-LIF. This
indicates that incorporating scale-consistent burst quan-
tization provides additional representational alignment
beyond standard integer spike encoding.
Effect of ReLSG-ET Surrogate
Finally, replacing
Box-ET with the proposed ReLSG-ET surrogate consis-
tently improves performance in both integer-based frame-
works (93.85% →94.45% for I-LIF and 95.05% →95.58%
for QB-LIF). This demonstrates that ReLSG-ET facili-
tates more effective gradient propagation for multi-level
spike learning.
Overall, the results verify that quantized burst encoding
contributes the major performance gain, while the pro-

5.4
Layer-wise Behavior of Quantized
Burst Representations
To analyze how quantized burst representations evolve
across network depth, Fig. 5 visualizes empirical burst-
level activation distributions in representative layers. Each
subplot corresponds to a trained model with its learned
quantization scale γ(ℓ) for that layer.
Since γ(ℓ) determines the discretization step from mem-
brane potential to burst level, it modulates the effective
dynamic resolution of spike responses. Depending on its
alignment with the membrane potential statistics of each
layer, different burst-level utilization patterns emerge. In
some layers, probability mass spreads across a wide range
of intermediate burst levels, indicating active multi-level
usage. In others, responses concentrate toward lower lev-
els with rapidly decaying tails, reflecting more restricted
dynamic resolution. These observations confirm that burst
quantization behavior is depth-dependent rather than uni-
formly distributed across the network.
We further quantify these patterns using the statistics
shown in Fig. 6. The learned quantized scale γ(ℓ) exhibits
a non-monotonic dependence on network depth. Corre-
spondingly, burst-level entropy varies across layers and
typically reaches higher values in intermediate stages of
the network. The elevated entropy indicates more active
utilization of available burst levels in those layers. Impor-
tantly, the measured entropy remains substantially below
the theoretical maximum log2(n + 1)
  
n=20 ≈4.39, sug-
gesting that burst capacity is selectively allocated rather
than uniformly saturated.
Despite increased multi-level utilization, neuronal spar-
sity is preserved. As shown in Fig. 6(d), layers with higher
burst entropy do not exhibit systematically higher acti-
vation ratios. This demonstrates that quantized burst
coding increases information density per spiking event
without inducing a proportional rise in firing frequency.
Moreover, most intermediate and deep layers retain a sub-
stantial number of effective burst levels (with probability
p > 10−2), ensuring representational flexibility without
enforcing uniform level usage.
Overall, these results indicate that quantized burst learn-
ing induces a structured, depth-dependent allocation of
dynamic resolution, enhancing representational efficiency
while preserving the event-driven sparsity characteristic
of spiking neural networks.
5.5
Energy Efficiency
Table 6 reports the estimated inference energy per image
on CIFAR10. All models are trained for 200 epochs under
identical settings. Energy is computed following the neu-
romorphic estimation protocol of Tang et al. [49], based
on floating-point operations (FLOPs) and synaptic opera-
tions (SOPs), assuming 12.5 pJ per 32-bit FLOP, 77 fJ per
32-bit SOP, and 3.7 pJ per sign operation. Memory access
and data movement costs are excluded, so the compari-
son reflects arithmetic energy under identical hardware
assumptions.
As Nmax increases, both SOP count and energy con-
sumption rise due to the higher number of burst-induced
synaptic events. For example, compared with binary spik-
ing (50.14µJ), QB-LIF with Nmax = 20 consumes 67.64µJ.
However, this increase accompanies a substantial accuracy
improvement from 90.50% to 95.58%. Importantly, the
energy growth is gradual and sublinear relative to the ac-
curacy gain. While SOPs increase by approximately 4.3×
from binary to Nmax = 20, energy rises by only 35%, owing
to the dominant cost contribution of FLOPs, which re-
mains constant across configurations. This indicates that
burst coding enhances information throughput primar-
ily through event-level modulation rather than structural
computation expansion.
Overall, QB-LIF achieves improved accuracy under a
modest increase in estimated energy, reflecting a controlled
trade-off between representational capacity and synaptic
activity.
6
Conclusion
In this study, we revisited burst spiking from an explicit
quantization perspective and proposed the Quantized
Burst-LIF (QB-LIF) neuron for efficient multi-level spik-
ing representation. By formulating burst emission as a
saturated uniform quantization process with a learnable
scale, QB-LIF enables layer-wise adaptive control over
spiking resolution. The absorbable scale strategy decou-
ples training-time flexibility from inference-time efficiency,
preserving strict accumulate-only execution on neuromor-
phic hardware.
In addition, the proposed ReLSG-ET
surrogate gradient stabilizes optimization in discrete multi-
level spiking spaces by maintaining consistent gradient
flow within the burst interval while suppressing instability
outside it.
Extensive experiments across static and event-driven
benchmarks demonstrate that QB-LIF consistently im-
proves accuracy under ultra-low latency settings while
retaining compatibility with integer-based neuromorphic
computation. These results confirm that adaptive quan-
tized burst representations effectively alleviate the infor-

Abstract: Binary spike coding enables sparse and event-driven com- putation in spiking neural networks (SNNs), yet its 1- bit-per-timestep representation fundamentally limits in- formation throughput. This bottleneck becomes increas- ingly restrictive in deep architectures under short sim- ulation horizons. We propose the Quantized Burst-LIF (QB-LIF) neuron, which reformulates burst spiking as a saturated uniform quantization of membrane potentials with a learnable scale. Instead of relying on predefined multi-threshold structures, QB-LIF treats the quantiza- tion scale as a trainable parameter, allowing each layer to autonomously adapt its spiking resolution to the underly- ing membrane-potential statistics. To preserve hardware efficiency, we introduce an absorbable scale strategy that folds the learned quantized scale into synaptic weights dur- ing inference, maintaining a strict accumulate-only (AC) execution paradigm. To enable stable optimization in the discrete multi-level space, we further design ReLSG-ET, a rectified-linear surrogate gradient with exponential tails that sustains gradient flow across burst intervals. Exten- sive experiments on static (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet) and event-driven (CIFAR10-DVS, DVS128-Gesture) bench- marks demonstrate that QB-LIF consistently outperforms binary and fixed-burst SNNs, achieving higher accuracy under ultra-low latency while preserving neuromorphic compatibility.
